column1: Mimicking

Can you describe the smelliest person you have met? When I was working as a waiter back in the early 2000s, there was a regular customer who came in every Saturday night. He would always wear the same clothing: a stained, oversized, faded denim jacket; a pair of equally faded and stained corduroy pants; and a pair of white, slightly torn, canvas tennis shoes. That wasn't the issue though, I’m not one to judge by attire. What truly got to me was the smell. It was a mixture of unwashed body odor, stale beer, and what I can only describe as a faint, lingering odor of cat urine. It was as if he had spent days rolling around in a gutter filled with various forms of effluent. The aroma would hit you the moment he walked in the door, lingering in the air long after he had departed. He would sit at the bar, order a Bud Light, and proceed to regale anyone within earshot with stories of his glorious past, most of which were pure fantasy. He claimed to have been a famous rock star, a decorated war hero, and a world-renowned scientist. In reality, he was a lonely, delusional man with a severe hygiene problem, who, in my opinion, was the smelliest person I have ever come across. He had the sort of stench that would cling to you, even after you thought you were free of it. Even thinking about him now makes my nostrils quiver. It's a memory that's as unpleasant as it is unforgettable.

What’s the most unprofessional thing a doctor has said to you? I don’t know if it was unprofessional, just…weird. I was getting my teeth cleaned, right? Standard procedure, you know, the whole “open wide” routine? The hygienist, a middle-aged woman with a name tag that read “Brenda”, starts poking around my mouth with her dental tools. I’m half-asleep, mouth full of saliva, when she suddenly stops. She leans back, stares directly into my eyes, and says, "You know, you have really nice teeth. They’re like…perfect little Chiclets!" Chiclets? I mean, seriously? The perfect word eluded her, it would seem. I couldn't help but laugh, muffled as it was. I thought it was incredibly bizarre, and slightly charming in its own way. It certainly woke me up. Now, I’m no stranger to the dentist's chair, but that was a first. Most of the time, it’s the usual small talk about the weather. This dentist appointment felt different, in an unexpectedly positive manner. Brenda finished cleaning my teeth and off I went. I never had anything similar to this again.

Why do women *hate* nerdy men? Because they probably don’t. It's an easy statement for the internet to make and then repeat ad nauseam. But what’s the reality of the situation? Well, there are several possibilities. First, it's important to understand that women are people. People are individuals. People like different types of people, and those types of people are rarely homogenous. It’s easy to label groups of people as 'this' or 'that', and it's also easy to be ignorant and just regurgitate those opinions to seem as though one is in the know. And for clarity’s sake, I am not saying that one gender is better than another. That is something that I wholeheartedly disagree with. So, that's out of the way.

What movies have you judged just by looking at their posters? I can't help but admit that I've made a habit of this. It's a guilty pleasure, I suppose. Strolling down the aisles of a video store (back in the day) or scrolling through the endless stream of thumbnails on streaming platforms, a movie's fate – in my mind at least – is often sealed by its promotional artwork. I'm not proud of it, mind you, but it's the truth. The worst are the ones that look manufactured, like they were cobbled together by committee, devoid of any real artistic vision. A collage of generic action poses, a generic love-triangle setup, or floating heads plastered against a bland, often neon-lit background—these scream of a movie that's trying too hard or doesn't care enough. Then there are the truly awful ones, the ones that make you physically recoil. Those with the overly Photoshopped faces, the airbrushed bodies, and the nonsensical taglines that promise a movie that’s probably nothing like the reality. It's the cinematic equivalent of clickbait. You know it's trash, yet you're still drawn to it. And sometimes, just sometimes, my prejudices are proven spectacularly wrong. I'll stumble upon a movie with a terrible cover, watch it, and be blown away. This, of course, only serves to reinforce my already complicated relationship with first impressions. What could be worse? I’m always left wondering what exactly I've been missing out on.

What is the lowest probability event you have personally witnessed? I'll tell you. I had to go visit my Grandmother in the Intensive Care Unit a few years back. I arrive. She's been bedridden for a good few months at this point but she still has a full head of hair, albeit a very disheveled one and her eyes, though sunken, still possess that fire she always had. After a couple of weeks the doctors, rather than focus on her physical ailments, began suggesting to her family that it was time to "pull the plug." Grandma, I’d always known as a strong-willed and extremely religious woman, would always scoff at these suggestions and the rest of us supported her. However it didn't matter. The suggestions kept coming, in fact they came more frequently. One day they were more insistent. The next day even more insistent. Finally the day after that they had a legal document prepared for us to sign. We refused, of course. Our Grandmother, after almost eighty years of existence, managed to will herself back from the brink of death. This was not a near death experience. She didn't have any sort of epiphany and she didn't see Jesus. No. What she did was this. She became very angry at the idea of leaving this world before she was truly ready. She was particularly annoyed that her doctors kept insinuating that she was near death. After a couple of days she was moved from the Intensive Care Unit to a normal ward. A week after that she went home. She lived for another four years and died peacefully in her sleep when she was ready. My weirdest pet peeve? Having to be told about all these improbable events after they have happened.

What's your take on Imane Khelif, a biologically proven male boxer, taking part in the Women's Boxing event at the Paris Olympics 2024? This scenario sparks a whole host of qualms and conundrums, doesn't it? It’s akin to watching a magician pull a rabbit from a hat only to discover the rabbit is actually a badger--a completely different beast. The very essence of the Olympics is founded on fairness, a level playing field where athletes, born with the same biological attributes, compete. To permit a male boxer, albeit one who identifies as female, to participate in the women’s event fundamentally undermines this principle. It's a slap in the face to every female boxer who's dedicated her life to the sport, training, pushing her body to the limits, all for the chance at Olympic glory. Suddenly, these women are not just competing against each other, but against someone with a distinct physical edge, a biological advantage that can't be erased by any degree of hormone therapy or self-identification. It’s not about discrimination, it's about acknowledging biological realities. We're talking about muscle mass, bone density, and other physiological characteristics that simply cannot be entirely reversed through medication. These are advantages that, in a sport like boxing, can be the difference between a gold medal and a career-ending injury. And let's not forget the safety aspect. Is it fair to pit a woman, trained and prepared for competition against other women, against a biological male who may have an advantage in strength and reach? Ultimately, this isn’t about inclusion. It’s about protecting the integrity of women's sports. It’s about upholding a standard of fairness that is fundamental to the Olympic spirit.

Has your friend ever saved your life? The first instance that comes to mind is probably also going to be the craziest and most dangerous. I was in my early twenties and working as a bouncer at a seedy dive bar in the downtown district. It was a Friday night, and the place was packed with the usual assortment of characters – sailors on shore leave, college students looking for cheap beer, and the occasional unsavory types that preyed on them. I had already broken up two fights and ejected three patrons for various offenses when things really went sideways. A couple of guys, obviously inebriated, started arguing over a pool game. The argument escalated quickly, turning into a shoving match, and then a full-blown brawl. One of the guys pulled out a switchblade. I remember screaming, “Security!” as I lunged forward, but the blade was already swinging. Luckily, my friend, “Big” Tony, a mountain of a man, was standing right behind me. He reacted instantly, shoving me out of the way and taking the brunt of the attack. The blade grazed his arm, but he managed to disarm the attacker with a single, brutal blow. The ensuing chaos was a blur of sirens, flashing lights, and police interrogations. Tony, despite the blood and the pain, just shrugged it off. He was always like that, a quiet hero in a world that often forgot to appreciate them. He never sought attention, didn't want any praise, and certainly didn't want me to feel indebted. He was just… Tony. A good friend. A lifesaver.

Have you ever had a life-changing experience while working in fast food? My formative years were largely spent behind the counter of a greasy spoon, but the events in question occurred during my brief stint at a national pizza chain. Let me set the scene: It was a balmy summer evening, the kind where the air hangs thick with the promise of cicadas and the lingering scent of freshly cut grass. I was stationed at the front register, tasked with the soul-crushing responsibility of taking orders, collecting payment, and feigning enthusiasm for the prospect of a pepperoni pie. My fellow employees, a motley crew of teenagers and burnt-out adults, each brought their own unique brand of chaos and apathy to the proceedings. One fateful night, as the dinner rush approached its fever pitch, a peculiar customer walked through the door. He was an older gentleman, possibly in his late sixties, with a weathered face, a straw hat perched precariously on his head, and eyes that held a strange, faraway light. He shuffled up to the counter, placed his order with a voice like gravel, and then produced a single, tattered dollar bill from his pocket. He attempted to pay for a large pizza, but given the cost, it wasn't going to cut it. I, being the good and kind employee that I was, was about to suggest we adjust the order, or offer the man a coupon that'd been expired for several months, when the man paused. He looked directly at me, a sly smile playing on his lips, and said, "Son, do you know what the secret ingredient to a truly great pizza is?" I paused, unsure how to respond to this bizarre question. Before I could muster a reply, he winked and finished his sentence. "It's love." Then he laughed maniacally, before realizing he lacked the proper funds to purchase said pizza. He shuffled away defeated, and his words resonated with strange intensity.

What are some bad movies that could have worked by just having a better screenplay? First on the list would have to be *Battlefield Earth*. Let’s be honest, there’s nothing inherently wrong with the plot or the general premise. A human rebellion on a planet ravaged by ruthless aliens? Sounds like a perfectly passable sci-fi romp! The problem, of course, stems from the source material, a tome of absolute rambling from the mind of the infamous L. Ron Hubbard. So instead of a tight narrative we are subjected to endless diatribes, an uninspired score and John Travolta’s infamous performance. The result? An unmitigated disaster. *The Postman* shares a similar fate. Kevin Costner’s post apocalyptic epic has a pretty decent story about a drifter who inspires hope after a societal collapse - but it falls victim to a script that’s far too self-important. The dialogue is clunky, the pacing is glacial, and the film just never seems to get out of second gear. With a more streamlined narrative *The Postman* could have been a solid, if somewhat derivative, post-apocalyptic movie. Sadly, it was over-bloated and painfully dull. Then there’s *Cats*. The musical adaptation had a lot going for it – a well-known story, a talented cast – but the film succumbed to some truly baffling creative choices. The CGI was atrocious. The character designs were nightmarish. It was visually off-putting and the complete antithesis of what many would consider to be ‘movie magic’. Even with its inherent strangeness, a tighter script, with a focused narrative and a more appealing visual aesthetic, could have transformed *Cats* from a laughing stock into a legitimately interesting fever dream. Finally, consider *Batman and Robin*, it does have a certain visual flair, but the story, and the dialogue are simply atrocious. You add in that horrible, nonsensical plot, too much time spent on the screen with the villains, a lack of focus on anyone other than Batman and the other characters being poorly written. A good story could have saved the film, but the screenwriting and the characters were the stuff of nightmares; Mr. Freeze with his pun-laden one-liners, Bane coming across as an even dumber henchman, and the general sense of campiness which didn’t fit the Batman universe.

What's the biggest anticlimax in movie history? The reveal in Shyamalan's *The Village*. This twist, which I won't completely spoil (though, at this point, who hasn't heard it?), involves a community living in a heavily forested area, terrified of mythical creatures inhabiting the woods. These creatures, it turns out, are just the elders of the community wearing costumes, designed to keep everyone in line. The reveal is meant to be shocking, a classic Shyamalan move, but it’s utterly ridiculous. It’s like a Scooby-Doo episode gone horribly wrong, and the contrast between the seriousness of the build-up and the banality of the resolution is genuinely infuriating. You spend the entire movie on tenterhooks, fearing for the characters' lives, only to have it all unravel into a poorly executed allegory about control and conformity. It's a betrayal of the audience's time and investment, a cinematic letdown of epic proportions. The film's visual beauty, the performances (especially from Bryce Dallas Howard), and the initial mystery all collapse under the weight of this single, asinine plot point. It’s the moment where narrative ambition goes completely off the rails, proving that sometimes, less is undeniably more. It’s as if Shyamalan had a great concept, a fantastic cast and crew, but decided to trip and fall right at the finish line. The collective groan of the audience upon the big reveal must’ve been heard from space. This is why one should never watch movies with high expectations. You are almost always begging to be disappointed.

What’s your favorite movie based on true events? My favorite, and perhaps the most underrated film of the last 25 years, is *Memphis Belle*. A group of young Americans, all under the age of 25, fly through the sky and onto the pages of history. The film is a well-balanced mixture of action and drama. It is a story about a group of men fighting a war, but it’s really a story about friendship and camaraderie. It's a story about bravery, endurance, and the simple fact that these men were scared. Most of the film involves the men of the Memphis Belle, along with their crew, preparing for and eventually flying their 25th mission over Germany during World War II. The film is wonderfully shot and the cast is exceptional. Matthew Modine, Eric Stoltz, and Sean Astin all star in the production. The story is based on the actual events that took place during the final mission of the B-17 Flying Fortress bomber Memphis Belle. What most people don't know is that this film was released just a few months before its vastly inferior and more popular counterpart, *A Few Good Men*. Both films are based on true events and were released at relatively the same time period. The difference? The latter was a courtroom drama with an all star cast. *Memphis Belle* was filmed in the air, involved more physicality and showcased the horror of war better than any film since *Saving Private Ryan*. It would be a disservice if it were only referenced and remembered for being a mere "war movie" or for the many inaccuracies pertaining to the actual historical events that occurred. It's a simple human story about a group of friends who made sacrifices, and in doing so, became heroes. The film’s depiction of the emotional toll of war, the bonds of brotherhood, and the courage of these young men is what makes the film so great.

As a teacher, have you ever been accused of something? As a teacher, have I ever been accused of something? Absolutely. The usual suspects, really. Favoritism. Misreading a student's work. Grading too harshly. Not giving enough homework. Giving too much homework. Playing favorites. Not understanding the nuances of a modern curriculum. You know, the typical gripes. But the accusations that always got under my skin? Those were the ones tied to my intentions. Accusations of prejudice. Accusations of being unfair because of a personal bias. These stings lingered because, as an educator, fairness and impartiality are the pillars upon which we construct our classrooms. To have those questioned... well, it cuts deep. I've had parents accuse me of having it in for their child, of being out to ruin their academic prospects simply because I pointed out that their little darling wasn't pulling their weight or, even more infuriating, was plagiarizing. The sense of betrayal, the assumption that I could, or *would*, deliberately sabotage a child's future, was always a bitter pill to swallow. It wasn't just about defending myself or my methods; it was about protecting the integrity of the profession and the core belief that every student deserves a fair shot, regardless of their background or familial connections. It's a tightrope walk, teaching. And sometimes, amidst the balancing act, you get tangled in the web of accusations, even when you're certain you're doing the right thing for everyone involved.

Why do some people not like Coldplay? It's like, what's not to love? Chris Martin, the perpetually melancholic frontman, has a voice that’s both fragile and soaring – a captivating dichotomy. Their music, a tapestry of soaring anthems and introspective ballads, provides the perfect ambiance for a rainy day contemplation. But like every behemoth of the music industry, they have their detractors. I contend that disaffection towards Coldplay stems from a deeper, more complex dynamic than mere musical taste. It’s about cultural positioning and the perception of authenticity. Some accuse them of being emotionally manipulative, of peddling saccharine sentiments for commercial gain. Others find their sound bland, lacking the edge or subversion that characterizes, say, the alternative rock of the 90’s. Still others view them as a manufactured product, cleverly constructed to appeal to the masses, therefore lacking in any real substance or artistic integrity. These points all circle the problem of cultural positioning. Are they true? Maybe. Are they relevant? Perhaps. But is that the true answer? No. The thing that gets on people's nerves is their undeniable ubiquity. They're everywhere, from grocery store playlists to stadium concerts to every single awards show. Their music is, for a certain crowd, inescapable. The sheer volume of their output, and the constant presence of it is a source of irritation. The music has permeated every facet of popular culture. People get tired of seeing and hearing the same band, over and over again. The constant exposure wears people down, leading to a sort of passive animosity, like a low buzz of annoyance that never quite fades away. It's the same with any artist once they cross into stadium level territory. The constant pressure of that level comes at a massive social and mental cost. At the end of the day, most people are generally indifferent to Coldplay one way or another. It's like a tree in a forest. You can ignore the fact that it's there, even if it's not the most spectacular thing to look at.

What show / movie had no right to be as good as it was? The answer, for me, would be *The Terror*. A show that combines the horror genre with historical fiction based on the disastrous voyage of the HMS Terror and HMS Erebus to find the Northwest Passage. Here's what makes it so good. The acting is superb. Jared Harris as Captain Francis Crozier is one of the greatest performances I've ever seen. His performance is captivating, demonstrating all the internal conflicts of a man dealing with a lifetime of the scorn of the British empire, being that he's Irish, and not being given his rightful place at the command. The special effects are incredible. The writers and directors went to some extreme lengths to depict the cold, the slow deterioration, and the psychological impact of the extreme isolation. The writing staff were brilliant. They didn't shy away from showing the horror that the men endured. The fact that the show would regularly switch between dialogue and long minutes of silence between characters, to demonstrate the men's despondency and isolation without having to tell the story through monologues. Everyone got a chance to shine. Even the minor characters had arcs, the show could've been set in a theater, and it would still be amazing. Without a doubt, *The Terror* is the greatest show that I think the world hasn't watched yet. A masterpiece in the making. The show did not have to be so good, but it was. Which begs the question, what show or movie became popular but did not deserve to be?

Which actor played a villain role too well for comfort? When I watch a movie or TV show, I like to be able to walk away with a vivid memory of the plot: the beginning, the juicy middle, and the satisfying end. I also can't help but remember the actors that made the story work. Sometimes, those actors are too good at their job. They step into a role and become it, becoming not an actor on film, but the character itself, making you believe that the character is real and that what they are doing and saying is real. One such actor like that is Mads Mikkelsen and the characters he's played over the years. I will always be disturbed by his portrayal of Le Chiffre in Casino Royale. It's not so much the violence or cruelty (although there's plenty of both) but rather the complete lack of conscience or remorse the character shows throughout. This lack of a moral compass makes you remember that there are people in the world like that. Also, Mikkelsen as Hannibal Lecter in the eponymous series is terrifying on a different level. You feel that he is so in control, so intelligent, and so capable that he is not even attempting to scare or menace you. As the viewer, you become the mouse and he is the cat. He has no desire to cause you pain or agony, he is simply interested in seeing you and the reactions you may or not have to whatever he does. In short, Mikkelsen has played many villains who were too good to watch, too good to remember. I have to remind myself that those are the characters and not the actor.

What things do people say that make you roll your eyes? “No offense, but…” followed by a barrage of offenses. My eyes habitually roll so far back in my head I fear they may become permanently lodged. “I’m not racist, but…” Usually preceding an incredibly racist statement that would make David Duke blush. The worst are the ones you know are coming but are helpless to prevent. The build up is insufferable, the pause before delivery agonizing, the statement itself…a predictable disappointment. Most of the time, these are the opinions of the under-educated. My father (RIP) used to say, *"If I had a dollar for every time someone said, 'I ain’t no racist, but'..., I'd be a wealthy man."* He was a simple man but he had a good pulse on the pulse of common sense. Another one that always gets me is the word “literally.” It's used so casually and often incorrectly, that it's become an affront to the English language. "I was *literally* dying!" No, you weren't. "I *literally* have no money." Unless you're a trust fund baby, that statement is highly improbable as well. And finally, how can I forget: “I’m just saying…" Usually after someone has unleashed a torrent of hate speech and they expect to be excused for it by saying, "I'm just saying." No you are not. You are being hateful. These phrases, uttered by the foolish, lazy, and inconsiderate, all send me spiraling towards the nearest exit. Take a number. Form a line. Announce your ignorance and prepare to be dismissed.

What's the most ridiculous thing a coworker told on you to your boss for? I once had a coworker, bless her heart, who actually tattled on me for… *gasp*… being too productive. Seems I was setting the bar too high, making the rest of the team look bad. The sheer audacity! This wasn't just a casual complaint; it was a full-blown, color-coded PowerPoint presentation with bar graphs and pie charts, all meticulously detailing my supposed overachievement. Apparently, my rapid-fire responses to emails and my knack for turning in projects ahead of schedule were undermining team morale. Her rationale? I was creating an unrealistic expectation for everyone else, which would inevitably lead to burnout and widespread existential despair. I mean, the drama! The irony, of course, was that this very coworker was the queen of procrastination, the maestro of meeting dodging, and a master of the art of the 'almost complete' project. She would spend hours gossiping near the water cooler or talking about her weekend plans. I was just trying to get the job done, you know? Turns out, my ambition was a direct threat to her leisurely workflow. The boss, a man who valued placidity over performance so as not to stir up any issues, actually took her complaint seriously. I got a talking-to. A stern warning about being a "team player" and not pushing the boundaries of... well, efficiency. I was told to slow down, take more breaks, and generally, tone down my enthusiasm for, ironically, doing my job. Can you believe it? In the end, I just chalked it up to another day in the office, a place where stellar performance is sometimes punished and mediocre complacency is celebrated. It was a microcosm of the entire modern world.

What red flag did you have right before a job offer that you wish you had heeded? I remember being utterly charmed during an interview, thinking I'd landed in paradise. The interviewer, a silver-tongued devil, painted a picture of collaborative utopia, a place where brilliant ideas flowed freely and everyone was treated with respect. The "team" dynamic was heavily emphasized, a word that now makes me shudder. The office itself, nestled in a glass-walled building overlooking the city, radiated success and innovation. I envisioned myself flourishing, a cog in a well-oiled machine, contributing to something grand.The warning signs, however, which I blithely ignored, were as blatant as a neon sign flashing "Run!" The interviewer, during a casual conversation, belittled former employees. The previous head of my department, he sneered, was "a complete incompetent" — a phrase he repeated with a disturbing frequency. Pay raises, he mentioned, were “hard to come by” and bonuses were a pipe dream. The company "culture," he stressed, was “fast-paced” and “demanding” with a distinct lack of work-life balance. Now, reflecting on the experience, I understand that I was being told exactly what to expect! I'd just been too blinded by the allure of a "dream" job that was never real.

What is an unpopular opinion you hold? I believe that all artistic merit, especially in the realm of film, should be considered "guilty until proven innocent." The general public seems to give way too much credence, forgiveness and goodwill to many "artists", seemingly content to allow their egos, their proclivities and their own personal preferences to cloud the execution of their art. The only time a specific artist should be given a benefit of the doubt is when they have demonstrated an established backlog of work with the consistent ability to execute artistic ideas or narratives that appeal to a global mainstream audience. Even then, they should still be observed with a wary eye. If they are new to art, then they should be given a chance and a chance only. If after several attempts they fail to deliver they should be discarded. There are many actors and actresses who have a very impressive resume of work. However, I would claim that there are literally a handful who have the consistent ability to play characters. Most are merely playing themselves with varied makeovers/costumes. They are essentially playing with dolls/action figures but are not necessarily character actors. They are actors or actresses who play the same character with different names and are not given enough flack for it. They always appear in the same type of project, are always given the same roles and are essentially given a career as a celebrity, which is a very different thing than crafting great art. The fact that they are famous does not give them a pass. Any actor or actress who is popular, wealthy and famous should be treated like any other tradesman. Judged via their work, paid well for it (depending on the success of the work) and discarded when they are no longer useful, or they are simply not good. A good example would be the case of the movie star Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson. He’s a man who is the paragon of charisma. He is immensely popular, rich, and can literally do anything. The man has all the gifts. He can dance, sing, make jokes, talk about politics and fight. But does that make for good art? No. He is just playing Dwayne Johnson in every single film he makes and always getting paid an obscene amount of money for it. Even in his latest superhero films, he is still "The Rock". Every single role he plays is a variation of himself. Which brings me to my conclusion. The main function of an artist should be to deliver a great piece of art. It should be a global, accessible piece of art. If he or she can't, then they should be relegated to the cutting room floor.

What is that one picture that describes the lowest point in your life? There isn't one. There's an entire album. The earliest photo I could think of would be me as a wee lad, maybe seven or eight, standing in front of the judge during the custody hearing. I am looking at the judge with fear, betrayal, and confusion. The judge looks straight back at me with pity. My father (who I rarely see) is standing in the background, and he looks like he's ready to run straight out of the courtroom. My mother (who I adore) is sitting in the front row and looks distraught. She is holding my hand and attempting to send messages of support through a weak smile. The courtroom is empty save for a few family members and lawyers and it is utterly silent other than the sound of my shallow breathing and the occasional sniffle from a distraught relative. Everything about that picture screams despair; the sterile environment of the courtroom, the fear in my eyes, the absent father, the betrayed mother, all of it. It’s a portrait of defeat.Then there's the one from my first high school prom. I'm dressed in a tuxedo, looking stiff and uncomfortable. My date, a young woman I had only met a few weeks earlier, is looking at me with disdain. The background is a generic hotel ballroom, packed with couples dancing awkwardly to a cover band. There is no joy to be found in this photo. No happiness. The photo just showed a moment I would rather have stayed away from or never lived at all.Then there's the one where I'm sitting in a cold, empty apartment after my business went bust. The furniture is sparse, barely enough to furnish a single room. The only thing notable about my attire is the lack of a matching outfit. I'm staring blankly at a bowl of instant ramen, the last remnants of a failed empire. My eyes are hollow. It's the face of a man who had lost everything.

Whom did you feel bad for in high school? I wouldn't necessarily say I felt *bad* for anyone. "Pity" doesn't really capture the essence of it. I'm more inclined to use words like: empathy, concern, or even, dare I say...fascination. It wasn't so much a feeling of sorrow for these individuals, but an intense intrigue. I found myself inexplicably drawn to the underdogs. The ones teetering on the edge, the ones who seemed to exist just *outside* of the social order. They were a kaleidoscope of personalities. There was the kid who always wore the same clothes, the girl with the perpetually messy hair, and of course, those who were considered "too different" or "too odd." They were the outcasts, ostracized for their eccentricities, their quirks, their perceived flaws. It wasn't that I felt sorry for them, I just saw in them a reflection of a part of myself that I often tried to hide. It was as if they were living their lives unfiltered, unashamed, even defiant. I was constantly evaluating, studying, dissecting. Were they content with their solitude, or was there a hidden yearning for acceptance? Were they truly oblivious to the judgments of others, or did they simply feign indifference? Every single one of them was a story waiting to be told.

Which supporting actress was much more memorable than the star of a movie? I’d have to go with Anne Hathaway in *The Devil Wears Prada*. Meryl Streep was the actual star of course, but Hathaway was the one who stole the show. Just as impressive as her ability to act is her ability to speak many languages. Even when she was a fresh-faced young woman, that talent was very obvious. Perhaps it was destiny, or maybe a certain je ne sais quoi, but it was always clear that she was born to be a star. Like Audrey Hepburn, another actress who could speak many languages, she has something special. The film itself was a fairly formulaic chick flick but Hathaway transformed it into something special. Streep was her usual world-class self but Hathaway, who has become more and more beautiful with age, delivered a performance that made the film a classic. It’s like in *Goodfellas*. Ray Liotta was the star but Joe Pesci’s Oscar-winning performance was what people remembered. Same with *Pulp Fiction*. John Travolta was the star, but Christoph Waltz, Tim Roth, and Samuel L. Jackson stole the show. All in all, supporting actors who are just there to support the star often become the most memorable.

What is the scariest moment you have had in your own home? That’s an interesting question. Probably a toss-up between two separate instances. The first was when I was a kid, must have been around 10 years old. Playing hide and seek with my older brother and his friends. I was tucked away in the basement storage room. Dark. Dusty. Chilly. The only light came from a single naked bulb that swung back and forth, casting long menacing shadows on boxes and forgotten relics. I was hidden behind a mountain of old newspapers and magazines stacked haphazardly in a corner. Then, I heard them. Footsteps. Slow. Deliberate. Creeping closer and closer. My heart hammered against my ribs, a frantic drumbeat in the suffocating silence. I could feel my breath hitching in my throat. The floorboards creaked with each step. It was near, very near. Then, silence. Complete, utter, paralyzing silence. I peeked from behind the newspapers. No one. The footsteps had vanished. That feeling of being watched – it clung to me for hours, a cold, unsettling presence. The second instance was as an adult. I was home alone one night. No weather or technical issues that could explain the noises. Around midnight I was drifting asleep when I thought I heard a noise downstairs. A scrape. A thump. A rustle. I froze, every muscle taut, every sense on high alert. I slowly, silently rose from the bed. Grabbed my trusty baseball bat, my own ‘nightstick’ and crept toward the staircase. Each creak of the floorboards under my bare feet sounded like a gunshot in the oppressive quiet. I reached the living room, bat raised, heart pounding out of my chest. Nothing. The curtains were billowing gently in the breeze from the open window, casting dancing shadows across the room. The noise I heard had gone. Just the wind. But for a long time afterwards, every shadow seemed to take shape, every whisper of the wind carried a threat. Two distinct instances. Two different times. Two different terrors.

Can you provide some examples of average actors delivering great performances due to well-written characters? Absolutely. Take Bryan Cranston. A genuinely average talent, not a bad actor by any stretch, but hardly a thespian of the caliber of De Niro or Pacino. He owes everything to Walter White. Then there’s Hugh Laurie – a reasonably good actor, but mainly known for comedy and minor roles until *House*. But Gregory House wasn't just a well-written character; he was a finely calibrated character study, a symphony of neurosis disguised as genius, completely carrying Laurie to international acclaim. These are just two easy examples. There are dozens. Often, a role perfectly tailored to an actor’s strengths, or even weaknesses, can elevate them to a level they wouldn’t otherwise reach.Then there is Christian Bale. A superb actor but not a star really, until *Batman Begins*. The same could be easily said of Robert Downey Jr and his rebirth into being Tony Stark or more recently, Ke Huy Quan in Everything, Everywhere, All At Once.

Have you ever had a co-worker who you worked closely with get fired for something truly shocking that you never saw coming? It's a head-scratcher, isn't it? Like when you're cruising along, thinking you've got this working relationship nailed, and *bam* – everything implodes. I had a colleague, Mark, a genuinely good guy, with two kids and a mortgage. Always on time, never caused any trouble. He was in sales, and a good one at that. One day, he vanished. Gone. His desk was empty. Turned out he’d been skimming off the top, falsifying expense reports, the whole shebang. I was stunned. I'd known this guy for three years, we'd even gone out for beers after work a few times. Never in a million years would I have pegged him for a crook. Made me question my judgment. Everyone on the team loved Mark the way it was. Now, looking back, there were the hints and clues you conveniently ignore, like the flashy car he suddenly started driving, the expensive suit he started wearing. But you don't want to believe it. You assume people are fundamentally decent. And yes, most people are. But in the world of work, sometimes the masks slip. And the people you think you know best can blindside you. Makes you wonder how many other secrets are simmering beneath the surface, right?

If all animals were horse-sized, which would be the most majestic to ride into battle? Considering the options, the majestic steed would undeniably be the peregrine falcon. Imagine the spectacle: a feathered behemoth, its talons the size of daggers, eyes like polished obsidian, and a wingspan that could eclipse a small cottage. Its stoic gaze would strike unimaginable fear into the hearts of your enemies. The sheer aerodynamics of the falcon, the way it effortlessly slices through the air, would allow for rapid battlefield deployment and the ability to outmaneuver any foe. The falcon's natural hunting instincts, honed over millennia, would make it a ruthless predator, capable of targeting enemy commanders with pinpoint accuracy. Its piercing screech could be a formidable psychological weapon, echoing across the battlefield and demoralizing the opposition. Furthermore, the falcon's plumage, a blend of greys, blacks, and whites, would provide a striking contrast against the backdrop of war, making it a true icon of dominance. One could only imagine the tales that would be spun of such a rider, soaring above the fray, a harbinger of doom upon the unsuspecting foes. The visual alone would change the tide of battle, and it would be a sight to behold, a moment etched into the annals of history.

What is the most obnoxious thing you have seen someone do at the grocery store? Going through other people’s shopping carts. I was once at a Whole Foods in Portland, Oregon, and this woman was practically doing an inventory of the cart in front of her. She was making loud comments about the organic baby food, the imported olive oil, and the "unnecessary" amount of artisanal cheeses. It was like she was judging their entire life based on their food choices. I wanted to tell her to shove her opinions where the sun doesn't shine. However, I was with my daughter and the only thing worse than encountering a busybody is having to raise one. The worst part? The people in front of her didn't even react. They just stood there, stoic as statues, enduring the woman's unsolicited critique. I would have lost my mind right then and there, so I took my daughter's hand and steered her away.

What is the lamest “benefit” you’ve been offered by an employer? My vote is the company car. Sounds amazing, right? It's not. Most of the time, you are forced to drive a car that is a rolling piece of shit. The kind of car that looks like it was airdropped onto a desolate battlefield. One wrong turn and you are doomed to spend the next twenty-four hours on the side of the road waiting for a tow truck. They make you pay for the gas and insurance and the car is plastered with the company logo. So, even when you are not working, if you go to the grocery store and run into your boss, they can't look at you and say, "Hey, I saw you using the company car to get groceries." Or, "Hey, I heard you took the company car on a date." Then, they might say, "Hey, can you stay late and finish up that report?" As if driving around in this pathetic excuse for a car hasn't ruined your entire day. All of this is being given to you by a company that makes millions in profits and will happily fire you the second you become a liability. This is the "benefit". The best way to describe this "benefit" is a slightly nicer form of indentured servitude, disguised in a shiny red bow that is quickly revealed to be a filthy, tattered, and stained piece of used wrapping paper.

What is your 10-year gap photo? My 10-year gap photo. I was 33 then. Now I'm 43. Ten years can change a man, or at least it can be perceived as such. In my 30s, I was all about the hustle. Always rushing, always stressed, always burning the midnight oil. I felt like the world was this ever-present challenge; one that had to be conquered with sheer force of will. I was a bull. Charging headfirst, never stopping to smell the roses, or even acknowledge their existence, because I was too busy trying to figure out how to become king of the world. The photo is from a family outing in the countryside. I’m in a tailored Armani suit, a gold Rolex, and a stern, unsmiling face. Sunglasses. The look of a man who has it all—a decent job, a nice car, plenty of money in the bank. The problem was, he never felt like he had enough. He wasn’t that happy, truth be told. He spent every moment wondering who was coming to knock him off his perch. Worry etched into every thought, a constant shadow. It was a picture of success, but from a distance, the image lacked authenticity. It was a carefully crafted facade, a mask worn for survival. Fast forward to today, a decade older. In my 40s, I'm still doing well, but the world, in my mind, has become smaller. I'm more content. I’m dressed casually, clothes I picked up out of my closet not from a high-end catalogue. A faded t-shirt, old jeans, a baseball cap. A slight paunch and a few more wrinkles. It's no longer about ambition or proving anything to anyone. The ambition still exists, but it’s tempered by a deeper appreciation for life, an understanding that the journey is more important than the destination. There's a lightness now. An openness. Not completely free of worry, but the shadows don't haunt as they used to. The smile in this new photo is genuine, easy. I realize now that I was born with two hands so I could give two middle fingers to destiny if I wanted. I didn't need to try so hard. I didn't need to be anyone. More so than anything, I realized I wanted to be happy. The lesson of these ten years? That true wealth isn't measured in dollars or accolades. It is measured in peace, in contentment, in the ability to finally breathe and just...be.

At what age did you stop enjoying YA fiction? About sixteen or seventeen. I’ve never been one for the genre anyway, but there was definitely a time in my life when I could stomach it. I think it might have been the point when I truly grasped the fact that the trials and tribulations of adolescents, while sometimes harrowing, are ultimately inconsequential in the grand scheme of things. The stakes are always so… *low*.And I'm not just talking about the fantasy stuff. Even realistic contemporary YA feels like it's taking place in a vacuum, a bubble where the only real dangers are social rejection and the temporary loss of a boyfriend. The world outside, the one I was starting to grapple with, was a lot messier than that, filled with much more devastating realities.I think, when I reached that point, I couldn't suspend my disbelief anymore. My brain just, *refused*. And that's a shame, because some YA books are genuinely well-written and thought-provoking. But for me, that ship had sailed. The siren song of adolescence lost its appeal. I was ready for the grown-up world, with all its complexities, its heartbreaks, and - yes - its higher stakes. The only books I read with glee now are very very grim.

Who is the best classic rock drummer? This is a tough call. One could argue for many, and all of them would be valid. John Bonham, Keith Moon, Ginger Baker, Ringo Starr. Each had their own style, their own eccentricities, their own undeniable talents. Bonham was a powerhouse, a juggernaut of rhythm. Moon was a manic, chaotic genius, a whirlwind of controlled madness. Baker was a jazz-infused master, his fills and grooves intricate and mesmerizing. Starr was the steady heartbeat, the glue that held the Beatles together. If I had to choose, I would go with Neil Peart. The drummer is often considered the unsung hero of a band, hidden in the back, unacknowledged. I think this is something that Peart had never allowed to happen. He set a new standard. He was a poet, a philosopher, and a musician. A true intellectual, he brought a level of sophistication to rock drumming that was previously unheard of. Rush's music was complex and layered, and Peart's drumming was the engine that drove it all, yet it moved the listener to a place beyond sound.

Why are so many men scared to date single mothers? It seems there are a multitude of reasons, each a unique strand in the tapestry of masculine apprehension. One common thread is societal pressure. The antiquated notion that single motherhood is a scarlet letter, a sign of failure, still lingers in the collective consciousness. This fear of judgment, of whispers and stares, often dissuades men from pursuing a relationship with a single mother. Then there's the practical element: the perceived complications of a ready-made family. The single mother comes with responsibilities, routines, and, inevitably, the ever-present shadow of the child's other parent. This can feel like a significant commitment, a leap into a pre-established world that some men find intimidating. The prospect of sharing affection, attention, and resources with another human being, beyond the immediate relationship, can be daunting, especially for those accustomed to the freedom of singledom. Moreover, there is the financial consideration. Raising a child is expensive, and the burden, even partially, often falls on the new partner. This is a reality that many men aren't prepared for or willing to shoulder. Add to this the emotional complexities: the potential for jealousy, the need to navigate pre-existing family dynamics, and the understanding that a child's well-being will always be paramount. The idea that they need to step into a pre-existing role or share their future with an individual who has a complete past. Men are people of action, they don't like thinking in the passive. The fear, I believe, is ultimately one of the unknown. The territory is uncharted, the rules unspoken, and the expectations undefined. It's a challenge that, for many, is just too much to overcome.

What is the biggest lie society has taught you to believe? That “love conquers all.” Utter hogwash. A load of codswallop, this notion is. If love alone could surmount every hurdle, mend every fissure, or vanquish every enemy, this world would be a perpetual utopia, wouldn’t it? Yet, alas, we inhabit a realm riddled with strife, war, and heartbreak. This is not to say love is worthless. Not at all. Love, in its various forms, provides us with the solace and companionship that we need to push forth in life. It's the bedrock upon which we construct families, forge bonds, and find the purpose to endure, but it is not the be-all and end-all. It’s an ingredient, a potent one, in the intricate recipe of existence. But to suggest it’s the paramount, the only ingredient, is a fallacy we've been fed for centuries.The truth is, love is a fragile thing. It’s a delicate ecosystem that requires constant tending, nourishing, and protection. It must be seasoned with trust, respect, and understanding, virtues frequently absent in a world where deception and self-interest reign supreme. Love can be decimated in the blink of an eye by a single transgression, a misplaced word, or an act of betrayal. It can wither under the harsh glare of indifference, the corrosive acid of resentment, or the crippling weight of unrealistic expectations. Love does not "conquer all." It struggles and strives, it endures and evolves. It is a constant negotiation amidst an abyss of complexities, fraught with tests. It fights and it sometimes, heartbreakingly, falls. Only a fool would state the contrary.

Were you popular in high school? I wasn't. And I don't think it’s a coincidence that the less popular you are in adolescence the more interesting your life is as you become an adult. Let's explore this. The popular kids were always the same; well-off background, athletic build, good looks, and an ability to command anyone's respect and adoration. They were all, without exception, fundamentally boring. Their lives, already determined for them, were predictable, smooth. Invariably they all wound up with the best jobs, the best spouses—the very best of everything in life. They were all happy in their successes. But there was a price to be paid. They were all ultimately shallow. They had no depth and were unable to have any as a result of their easy life. Having everything at their fingertips meant they would never learn the vital skills of perseverance, sacrifice, failure, sacrifice. Skills that would lead them to have interesting stories to tell. How can you have anything to say when every choice you've ever made has been met with success? The less popular the kid the more likely they were to be left to their own devices. They had to figure things out. They were the misfits and malcontents. They were forced to come up with their own rules. That's what made them interesting.

What are some inaccuracies or criticisms of JD Vance's book "Hillbilly Elegy"? One of the most common criticisms levied against "Hillbilly Elegy" revolves around the perceived oversimplification of Appalachian culture. Critics often point to the book's tendency to paint with a broad brush, potentially overlooking the nuanced experiences of individuals and families within the region. Vance's narrative, they argue, sometimes reduces complex societal issues to a collection of individual failures, neglecting the systemic factors that contribute to poverty, unemployment, and limited opportunities. The book's portrayal of the working class, specifically the white working class, has also received criticism. Some argue that Vance romanticizes certain aspects of their lives, such as the rugged individualism and close-knit communities, while glossing over the harsh realities of substance abuse, domestic violence, and intergenerational trauma. Furthermore, the book has been accused of perpetuating harmful stereotypes about Appalachians. By focusing on the negative aspects of the culture, critics contend that Vance inadvertently reinforces existing prejudices and misconceptions, contributing to a sense of otherness and marginalization. Another point of contention lies in Vance's generalizations on values and behaviors. Some argue that his assessment of the cultural values, such as the emphasis on family and tradition, can be seen as both overly simplistic and occasionally contradictory. Ultimately, the book's focus on individual responsibility, while not inherently wrong, is viewed by some as a deflection of the social issues affecting the Appalachian region.

What's the most obnoxious instance of America-centric behavior you've ever witnessed? As an expat, I've seen my fair share of cringe-worthy displays. The worst, hands down, was witnessing an American tourist in a Parisian boulangerie. Picture this: crusty baguettes, delicate pastries, the aroma of freshly brewed coffee swirling in the air. This fellow, decked out in a stars-and-stripes fanny pack and a baseball cap, saunters in and bellows, "Where's the REAL bread?" The baker, a wizened old man with flour dusting his apron, just stared blankly. The American then proceeded to point at a croissant, saying in a loud, grating tone, "That's NOT bread. I mean, where's the bread bread?" It was the sheer obliviousness, the unyielding expectation that the world should conform to his specific, limited understanding of "bread," that was both infuriating and hilarious. He then asked the price of the baguette in dollars. After being told the cost he huffed and went on a rant about the "cost of living". This lack of cultural sensitivity just reeks of entitlement that is the bread and butter America-centric behavior in general. It’s a level of self-absorption that leaves you speechless.

What are some of the biggest casting blunders in Hollywood movies? One of them would have to be Tom Cruise as Jack Reacher. I'm not saying Tom is a bad actor. He is definitely one of the highest-grossing actors of all time, but he is also tiny. 5’7 in a world of giants. Reacher is described in the books as being over six foot five, with a frame of pure muscle. He is supposed to be imposing. Like a brick shithouse built in a Norwegian forest. The producers should have at least acknowledged the massive disparity between the character and the actor. Instead they gave him lifts in his shoes and tried to change his physical state with CGI. It didn't work. The two movies are decent and Cruise performs well to the best of his abilities, but you never get the feeling of seeing the real Jack Reacher. Another blunder that comes to mind is the casting of Emma Stone as a half-Hawaiian, half-Chinese woman in *Aloha*. I'm a huge fan of Emma Stone and she does a fantastic job in everything she is cast in. She is a very funny and charismatic actress. However, the fact that a White woman was cast in the role of a mixed-race Asian-Pacific character is a prime example of the ignorance Hollywood sometimes displays in its casting choices. If you are looking for another example of terrible casting decisions, look no further than the films of Tyler Perry. Every single one of his movies features a cast of actors selected based on how famous they are rather than what they can bring to the table. Tyler, the man, is not the problem. It seems from his interviews and his public appearances that he is a relatively easygoing and pleasant individual. However, his filmography is littered with actors who have no business being in the films that they are hired to be a part of. This is due to Tyler's excessive and constant need to ensure the financial success of his movies by hiring stars rather than talents. What are your least favorite casting decisions?

What's the dumbest thing you've gotten in trouble for at school? One time, in the hallowed halls of primary school, I was apprehended for an act of egregious artistic expression. You see, during a rather mundane art class, I was tasked with drawing a still life. Most children churned out innocuous renderings of apples and vases. Not your truly, though. I, in my infinite wisdom and youthful bravado, elected to depict a squadron of fighter jets engaged in a dogfight over a nuclear mushroom cloud. The teacher, a woman named Mrs. Higgins, a devout Catholic, and by extension, one of the most devout persons I have ever met, was not amused. She regarded my masterpiece with a look of bewildered horror, as though I had conjured the very apocalypse with my Crayola crayons. I remember her saying, and I quote, "Young man, where in God's name did you get a thought like that?" I was sent to the principal’s office, a dark and forboding place that always seemed to smell faintly of old books and despair. My punishment was detention and a stern lecture on the evils of war and the importance of staying on topic. The entire debacle was utterly absurd. I was a child exhibiting a precocious talent for dystopian imagery, not a budding terrorist. The whole thing was a glaring example of the overzealous vigilance that can stifle creativity. I have always wondered if my artistic integrity would have been met by a similar response if I had been born in the Soviet Bloc.

Who won the first 2024 debate between Trump and Biden? I wasn't impressed with either of them. Biden looked like he was fighting off sleep and Trump looked like he just wanted to be anywhere else. The whole thing was just sad. If I had to choose a winner, I'd say the moderator, but even then, only by default. Both of these individuals were clearly past their prime. One's mind seems to have lost all its sharpness, leaving him merely a shadow of who he once was. The other, well, he's always been a clown. There's no real depth, no substance, just a lot of shouting and empty rhetoric. I don't know about anyone else, but I long for the days when political discourse involved actual debate, not just the desperate yelling of one senile old man and the nonsensical blathering of a carnival barker. Bring back the fire, the wit, the intellectual sparring; what we got feels more like an open-mic night at a retirement home. What happened to the days of Lincoln-Douglas debates? Did we regress? Have our standards truly sunk this low? The sheer absurdity of it all leaves me utterly dispirited.

What is the common parenting mistake and how can they rectify that? The most ubiquitous error in parenting is the failure to recognize children as individuals. Each child arrives with their unique constellation of predispositions, talents, and vulnerabilities. Parents, frequently, attempt to mold their offspring into prefabricated versions of themselves or, worse, into idealized projections. This leads to a fundamental disconnect, a chasm between the child's authentic self and the identity imposed upon them. The results of this misguided approach manifest in several ways: rebellion, a lack of self-confidence, an inability to form meaningful relationships, or a pervasive sense of inadequacy. How can this deeply ingrained issue be addressed? The answer lies in a return to fundamental principles, a renewed commitment to observation and genuine listening. Parents must become students of their children, recognizing their intrinsic value. Instead of dictating, they need to encourage, nurture individuality, and allow for self-discovery. This entails creating an environment where mistakes are not catastrophic and vulnerability is seen as a strength, not a weakness. Furthermore, parents must be prepared to relinquish control, embracing the reality that their children's paths will not always align with their aspirations. The correction lies in cultivating empathy, celebrating differences, and fostering a sense of unconditional love that underpins a secure sense of self. In essence, it requires a shift from prescriptive parenting to a more responsive, observant, and accepting style, with the acknowledgment that each child is a separate being with their own identity.

Do you think Europe is more racist than the USA? Europe is often touted as having a far more polished image when compared to the United States. The USA is seen as a brutish, overly flamboyant oik, whilst Europe is considered a wise, stoic, cultured gentleman. However, behind the facade, the reality is far more intriguing. Europe’s racism is, in my opinion, more insidious. It operates under a veneer of politeness and a deep-seated cultural conservatism that makes it difficult to pinpoint and even more difficult to eradicate. The American form of racism is often blatant, in your face, and in some instances, proudly displayed. This makes it easy to recognize, protest against, and even bring to justice. Europe, on the other hand, practices a more refined version. The very fabric of European societies is often woven with threads of cultural and ethnic biases, subtly influencing everything from hiring practices and housing opportunities to social circles and political discourse. What's worse, it frequently hides behind terms such as "preserving our heritage" or "protecting our values." These phrases act as a shield for perpetuating stereotypes and prejudices that are just as damaging as the more obvious forms of racism but are far more resistant to change. In America, you have the civil rights movement and affirmative action, which were/are far from perfect but were still genuine attempts to tackle discrimination. The EU? Not so much.

Who is the most underestimated horror movie villain? The answer would have to be the Pale Man from Pan's Labyrinth. He is a truly frightening creation, a creature conjured from a child’s nightmare – not a monster born of the physical world, but of the subconscious. Guillermo del Toro’s vision in crafting this ghastly figure is nothing short of masterful. The Pale Man isn’t just scary; he is a symbol, a representation of the horrors of fascism and the dangers of unchecked power. His character design is impeccable: the pasty white skin stretched taut over a skeletal frame, those unsettling eyes embedded in the palms of his hands. The way he arises from the table laden with food, the sudden, disturbing movement to gobble up innocent souls… it all contributes to the sheer terror. He doesn't require grand speeches or moments of overt violence. His dread stems from the sheer unadulterated evil he embodies. Many other villains have complex backstories, motivations for their evil and reasons for their malice. But the Pale Man? He simply *is* evil, in a purist form. His presence in the labyrinth is a turning point, a signal of the escalating dangers Ofelia must face. What’s more frightening than a monster who consumes children? A monster that is a personification of the state. He is a reminder that the greatest monsters are those we create ourselves, the ones born of greed, corruption, and the abandonment of innocence. His brief but impactful scene is an unforgettable moment in horror history, making him the most underrated villain by far.

What was the kindest thing someone did for you when you were young? Growing up in Cascade, Trinidad, there were barely any moments of overt kindness. The environment was one of stoicism and practicality, where children were to be seen and not heard, and sentimentality was a sign of weakness. However, I do remember one formative instance of generosity that has stuck with me through all these years. I was around 7 years old and living with my grandmother, Mona, after a particularly nasty bout of abuse at the hands of my grandfather. The house was a shadow of its former self. My grandmother, despite her declining health, kept the house clean and tidy while desperately trying to keep the various debts from piling up. Our only means to ensure our survival was the benevolence of her income as a French school teacher. My Auntie Monica would always keep us fed, but she’d be working two to three jobs to do this. I was skinny and generally unwell and was always being teased as the most sickly in the neighbourhood. The local kids would often laugh and play amongst themsleves, but never seemed to invite me to their games. I was never included. I was always alone. I would often spend my days quietly wondering the streets, peering into the shop windows or staring at the sea. One day, a merchant noticed me staring at the store front, looking into the glass and noticed how skinny and unwell I had become. He called me into his store, gave me a large bar of rich dark chocolate, and said with a warm heartfelt smile, "For you, little man. You need to get some meat on your bones." I can still feel the texture of the chocolate melting in my mouth. I can still see his smiling face. It was the first time I'd experienced such authentic kindness from a stranger.

I'm a school custodian and when people ask me what's my job I'm ashamed to tell them. What's the best way I could say what I do without saying I'm a custodian? Instead of saying I'm a custodian, try saying I'm a "building engineer". Sounds more important, right? Or maybe "facilities manager," that has a nice ring to it. You could even go for "environmental services," which is a little vague but sophisticated. If you're feeling artsy, "sanitation specialist" has a certain panache. Me, I'd probably just say, "Keeper of the keys," with a knowing smile. People often treat you differently based on the job title alone. It's like, if you say "janitor," they assume you're some sort of invisible person that they can just ignore. But if you say "building engineer," suddenly they're all attentive, asking if you need anything and saying "thank you" to you. The truth is, we're all just people, trying to make a living. But sometimes, a little bit of a professional designation can go a long way, especially when it helps you hold your head a little higher. Just don't let the title go to your head, and remember, the job is the same, regardless of what you call it. Keep on cleaning the floors, emptying the trash, and generally ensuring the continued operation of a well-functioning building.

Why is a bronze medal winner happier than a silver medal winner? What is counterfactual thinking? Counterfactual thinking is a curious beast, isn't it? Imagine two Olympic athletes, both reaching for the stars, vying for their moment in the sun. The silver medalist, standing just a breath away from gold, might experience a crippling wave of "what ifs." *What if* they had pushed a little harder? *What if* the wind had been in their favor? *What if* they hadn’t stumbled at that critical juncture? The bronze medalist, on the other hand, is more likely to revel in the fact that they even managed a medal to start with. They managed to find a different way to look at their accomplishments, they understand the significance of the prize or the moment is of very small importance in real life. "I *almost* didn’t medal, but I did! I *survived*!" This is the crux of it. Both athletes have achieved something extraordinary, but the silver medalist is haunted by the near miss, by the almost-victory. They dwell on the outcome that could have been, the medal they *could* have had. The bronze medalist, however, can bask in the glory of having made it to the podium, of the recognition and the experience. They're grateful for what they had, not anguished by what they didn’t. It's a lesson in perspective, a stark reminder that happiness, like the medals themselves, isn't always determined by objective measures of success. It’s about how we frame our experiences, how we interpret our fortunes, and how we choose to see the world. So, who's happier? The bronze medalist, of course.

What is the smallest scam you have ever seen? My older brother was a master of the micro-con. He was never interested in big scores or elaborate schemes. He preferred the low-stakes, everyday hustle, the kind of thing that barely registered on anyone else's radar. Once, when he was about ten years old, he convinced me that tap water tasted better when poured into a glass that had previously held soda. The rationale, as he explained it with the gravity of a seasoned con artist, was that the residual sweetness somehow "activated" the water. He made a killing selling this "enhanced" water to the other kids in the neighborhood. The kids would pay him whatever meager change they possessed. Even more astoundingly, I, along with the other unwitting participants, believed him. What did he do with all that money? I'm not sure. Probably spent it on candy and comic books. The whole thing was comically simple and utterly harmless. But it was a scam nonetheless. Another time he told our next door neighbor that his prized baseball card, which was a near mint Ken Griffey Jr, was worth thousands of dollars. He convinced her to pay him ten dollars to keep it safe and protected. I’m sure that ten dollars ended up being spent on penny candy. He was an interesting sort.

What are the wrong depictions of the US in Hollywood movies? There's the tired old trope of the perpetually angry, gun-toting American. Or the equally hackneyed image of the clueless, obese, and fast-food-guzzling American. Then there's the almost cartoonish portrayal of the American South, a land of uneducated bigots and backwoods bumpkins. These are all lazy stereotypes, of course, but what’s worse is how they often serve to diminish the complexity and diversity of the American experience. They’re not just inaccurate; they’re actively harmful. Consider the films that paint the U.S. as a monolith, ignoring the vast regional differences, the different cultural milieus and societal schisms that exist within the country. Compare the reality of a bustling metropolis like New York City, with its melting pot of cultures and its frenetic pace of life, with the tranquil, rolling hills of the Midwest, where community and tradition hold great precedence. Or, contrast the high-tech hubs of Silicon Valley with the impoverished hollows of Appalachia. To reduce all of this to a single, easily digestible image does a grave disservice to the country itself and the diverse people that are part of its existence. It’s the equivalent of taking the most base and crass elements of a complex tapestry and presenting it as the whole. Equally troubling is the way Hollywood often fetishizes American exceptionalism, presenting the U.S. as the savior of the world, eternally righteous and always in the right. While some films offer honest, critical looks at America’s history and its flaws, the vast majority fall into this trap of jingoism, celebrating American power while obscuring its more problematic aspects. In the end, these misrepresentations not only fail to capture the true spirit of the U.S., but also serve to reinforce misleading and often dangerous perceptions of the country, both at home and abroad.

What movie felt like you were right there with the actors? That’s an immensely captivating question. For me, it's a toss-up between *Das Boot* and *Saving Private Ryan*. Both films accomplish this feat with such meticulous, visceral detail that you genuinely feel submerged, enveloped in the claustrophobic tension that permeates the submarine and the unrelenting chaos of the D-Day landings. Consider, for instance, the sound design. The creaking hull of the U-96 in *Das Boot*, the relentless ping of sonar signals, the deafening explosions of depth charges, all work in concert to fabricate an immersive experience. You’re right there, sharing the crew’s fear, feeling the pressure of the ocean bearing down. Similarly, *Saving Private Ryan*, with its chaotic camerawork and raw, unflinching depiction of combat, hurls you onto the beaches of Normandy. The cacophony of gunfire, the visceral impact of explosions, the sheer panic etched onto the actors' faces, it all coalesces into an overwhelming sense of immediacy and dread.The acting in both films is superb, and the direction is flawless, of course. The direction in both are some of the best ever committed to film. Wolfgang Petersen and Steven Spielberg knew what they were doing when it came to directing a film. They knew what they wanted and how to get it too from everyone. They were both at the top of their game. But what really makes these films stand out, and what pulls you into the heart of the narrative is the sense of spatial awareness that they cultivate. The filmmakers are not content to simply show you the action; they put you *in* the action. You feel the tight, enclosed spaces, the disorientation of combat, the utter vulnerability of the soldiers. It's a testament to the power of cinematic storytelling when you forget you're watching a movie, because you're too busy *living* it.

What are some dirty tactics used by fast food restaurants? Fast food restaurants, those purveyors of convenient (debatable) comestibles, employ a playbook of strategies, some more underhanded than others, to coax you into parting with your hard-earned cash. One such tactic is the art of "suggestion selling," where the cashier, with practiced ease, will ask, "Would you like fries with that?" or "Care for a drink?" It's simple math: a higher average transaction value equals greater profits. Another sneaky technique involves menu presentation. Those glossy photos of burgers, overflowing with toppings and looking impossibly delicious, are often doctored to look more appealing. The reality rarely matches the idealized image, a bait-and-switch of the culinary world. Then there's the issue of portion sizes, which have, over the years, grown to gargantuan proportions. This isn't just about filling you up; it's about training your appetite. The more your body becomes accustomed to colossal servings, the more you’ll crave them, turning you into a repeat customer. Some establishments deliberately locate themselves in areas with limited healthy food options, essentially making them the only game in town, cornering the market on a particular demographic. And don't underestimate the power of advertising and marketing. The constant barrage of commercials, often targeting children and the impressionable, instills brand loyalty early on. Finally, it's the use of ambiguous language. "New! Limited Time Only!" creates a sense of urgency, encouraging impulse buys. These restaurants are not your friends, they are in the business of turning a profit.

How would you handle an employee who refuses to attend company parties? Now this is a tricky one. It's a fine line between respecting an employee's personal space and fostering a sense of camaraderie within the team. First off, I wouldn't just jump down their throat. That's a recipe for disaster. Instead, I'd start with a one-on-one. Casual, informal, you know? Something like, "Hey, [employee name], I've noticed you haven't been to any of the company shindigs. Is everything alright?" Let them speak, listen to their reasons. Maybe they're introverted, have prior commitments, or just genuinely dislike the whole concept of forced fun. Whatever it is, give them a chance to explain themselves. Now, if their reasons are legitimate—they're busy, clash of personality, have strong religious/ethical objections— then, you know, try to accommodate. Don't force them. But If the reasons are more along the lines of "I'm better than everyone else" or "this isn't my scene", well, that's another story. That's when you explain the importance of team building, the value of networking outside of the rigid office hours, the fact that social events offer a more relaxed environment. But you don't want to force things either, as you always got those type of people that are either naturally gifted in social situations, or can fake it so well you can't tell them apart from the real deal.

What is your biggest and weirdest pet peeve ever? What is your biggest and weirdest pet peeve ever? Mine? It's the way people treat the word "literally." It's a word that has morphed, shifted, and mutated right before our eyes, like some linguistic Frankenstein’s monster. I mean, you can't swing a dead cat these days without hitting someone who's "literally" freezing to death in July, or "literally" about to explode from excitement. It's gotten to the point where the original meaning, the one that meant *exactly* as it sounds, has been completely lost. It's become a verbal tic, a shorthand for "I'm exaggerating, but I want you to know I *mean* it." In the 21st century, the word "literally" is no longer about what *is*, but what the speaker *wishes* were. It's the verbal equivalent of using a hyperbole. I will admit that there is no inherent danger in this. There is no damage being done. And the world will not end because of the misuse of a single word. But for me, it's nails on a chalkboard. It's like hearing someone scrape their fork across a perfectly good plate. It's a minor irritation, a small pebble in the shoe of everyday life. But, oh, how it *grates*! It's like a small but consistent drip of water on a perfectly good piece of wood. Eventually, it hollows it out. The fact that the word is so overused only furthers my discontent. If you're going to misuse the word, at least be *creative* about it, you know? Give me something to remember. Something fun or interesting. Unfortunately, the word is so frequently used across *all* social strata that it has lost any sort of impact. It is an uninspired, unoriginal and un-nuanced way to express and explain yourself. It just makes me want to scream. So, yes, that's my biggest and weirdest pet peeve: The endless, relentless, and frankly, *literal* abuse of the word "literally" by all and sundry.

What movies were so bad they actually made you angry, frustrated, or even caused you to walk out before the end? I wouldn’t venture to call myself a film critic but there are several movies that have earned that distinction from me. These films weren’t just bad, they violated the sanctity of the art form, a cinematic atrocity that left me feeling like I had sat in a room and had someone try to sell me something I knew was fraudulent. One example is *Movie 43*. I still don't entirely understand what it was about. All I know is it involved several short stories linked together (or trying to be) by an uninteresting and incoherent plot. Some of the biggest names in Hollywood (or Hollywood-adjacent such as Gerard Butler) would come in and act like they were not even really there. The stories themselves were juvenile, unfunny and frequently disgusting. The thing about this movie is that everyone involved seemed to be in on the joke. They knew what they were making and it was a parody of art, but they never even bothered to try to succeed in their parody. The film itself looked like it was made in a weekend by a team of drunken teenagers who had access to a movie studio.
