Another example is *Cats* the musical, not that it even deserved to be called a movie. Why do they want to make everything into musicals now anyway? It’s really lazy, and I’m not entirely sure why, but the people that love musicals are generally stupid and would consume anything. The CGI looked bizarre, like a poorly rendered video game with a budget that was beyond anything I could ever imagine. Every actor looked the part, but as soon as they opened their mouths it was clear this cinematic exercise in greed was designed to bilk the audience. The actors may as well have just sung the dictionary. I walked out before the end of both of those movies. I felt the need to protect my mind.

What are some plot holes in some of famous movies? When it comes to cinematic inconsistencies, the tapestry of Hollywood is often threaded with glaring oversights, factual inaccuracies, and illogical leaps. Take, for instance, the iconic film *Back to the Future*. The very premise of temporal displacement hinges on an intricate web of paradoxes, none more glaring than Marty McFly's near-erasure from existence. If his parents never meet, he vanishes. Yet, his actions in the past are what set his parents on the path to love in the first place. It's a mind-bending conundrum. Time travel, in this instance, acts more like a rubber band stretched to near breaking, than something governed by the rules of physics. Then there's the issue of Doc, who built a time-traveling DeLorean, powered by nuclear material and, later, lightning, in a cluttered garage with only basic tools. The sheer improbability of such a feat challenges our suspension of disbelief. Not to mention the logistical nightmare of acquiring plutonium in 1955 without raising any suspicion. The brilliance of the film lies in its ability to distract us by means of witty dialogue, dynamic characters and ingenious set-pieces from even contemplating a lot of the holes. In *Jurassic Park*, the science itself is riddled with fault lines. The notion of resurrecting dinosaurs from fossilized mosquito blood is a leap of faith, even within the context of a fantastical adventure. Furthermore, the dinosaurs, brought to life in a controlled environment, quickly demonstrate a level of intelligence and adaptability that undermines the concept of genetic engineering. The velociraptors, in particular, are portrayed as cunning, problem-solving predators, capable of opening doors – a sophistication that stretches the boundaries of plausibility. These plot holes don’t detract from the films' successes, but they do stand as testaments to the lengths filmmakers will go to entertain us, and where scientific rigor is often sacrificed at the altar of a good story.

What actors were supposed to be the next best thing in Hollywood but never made it? There are so many. This is going to be a long one. Where do I begin? Let's start with the obvious choices. Freddie Prinze Jr. handsome, charismatic, and the star of the 90s/early 2000s. Sure, he's still around but he's relegated to voice acting and occasional cameos. How about the poster boy for the 80s, Rob Lowe? Loved by many, idolised by some. The embodiment of youthful charm and good looks. Yet he's always been more known for his exploits outside of acting than his performances. And then there's Cuba Gooding Jr. Oscar winner, starring in many iconic films for a few years there. After a certain period of stagnation, every movie he's starred in has been low budget and unmemorable. I mean, it's not like the man just became a bad actor overnight. He just stopped getting good roles! And what about Ryan Phillippe? Another 90s heartthrob. Handsome, talented and still capable of turning in good performances, but is he a household name? Not quite. The entertainment landscape certainly has been a cruel mistress toward these talented individuals.

What do fast food employees think of customers who come in frequently, say, multiple times a week or even daily? I’ve spent many years working in the fast-food industry and, as such, have developed a solid perspective on this peculiar dynamic. The short answer? It's a mixed bag. There's a certain breed of customer, the regulars, who become, in a warped sense, quasi-friends. You learn their names, their orders, and the specifics of their day, often before they even utter a word. These are generally the easier customers to deal with, their predictability offering a sense of comfort in the chaotic reality of the food service world. Then the other end of the spectrum, however, presents a considerably thornier proposition. It is, of course, the incessant, almost invasive customer. The person who demands extra napkins, modifications to the order which are bordering on the ridiculous, and questions everything, including the nutritional value of a soda. These patrons are almost universally loathed. They are the reason for every eye roll, deep sigh, and the occasional, muttered, expletive under the breath. You become wary, because their frequent visits rarely signify genuine patronage; they're more often symptoms of a greater need, a hunger far beyond the physical. But, in all veracity, no matter your personal feelings, their consistency means you're more likely to survive your shift. So the regulars? They are generally welcomed. The overbearing, demanding, and relentless? We’ll see how they treat the next customer.

What is legal but ethically wrong? Here's something that’s a real head-scratcher: the way we treat animals in factory farms. Think about it. It’s perfectly legal in many places to cram them into tiny cages, deny them sunlight and fresh air, and pump them full of hormones to make them grow faster. This may be legal, but is it right? Is it ethical? Absolutely not. Take the life of a chicken. A caged chicken’s life is often a living hell. No room to move, no access to the outside world, no chance to express their natural behaviors. Now, I might be a city man, but even I know a chicken deserves more than that. If you think about it, a lot of things fall into this grey area.

Which extremely surreal film would you consider to be worth watching? David Lynch's *Eraserhead*. A true visual symphony of the unsettling and the bizarre. The narrative, if you can even call it that, is a descent into the subconscious, a nightmare made manifest in grainy black and white. The film oozes with an oppressive atmosphere, a feeling of unease that burrows deep into your soul. Every frame is meticulously crafted, a testament to Lynch's unique artistic vision. The industrial soundscape is equally crucial, creating a chorus of unsettling noises that further disorient the viewer. It's not a film for the faint of heart, mind you. It's challenging, perplexing. But for those willing to embrace its strangeness, *Eraserhead* offers a profound cinematic experience unlike anything else. It's a film that stays with you long after the credits roll, prompting you to question the boundaries of reality and dream. Just be prepared to lose a little sleep, and perhaps a fragment of your sanity, in the process. One of the greatest movies ever made, it's on par with some of the hardest films ever made. Consider adding it to your list.

Without saying their name, who is your favorite fictional character? Mine is a toss-up between two. The first is a beautiful elven assassin with long dark hair and an affinity for archery. She has a cold, calculating demeanor, but deep down, she possesses a surprising vulnerability. The second is a disgraced jedi knight haunted by the ghosts of his past, struggling with the dark side and trying to find redemption. He is conflicted, tormented, and incredibly complex. The first tends to bring out the most savage side of me, whereas the second brings out the paternal side. I am always torn between the two. But there is something very telling regarding these two characters. Both have some unique attributes. Both have an unmatched set of skills yet their paths are wrought with pain, anguish, and loneliness. This leads into another question. What is more powerful than having unmatched skills? Well, to answer that, let's go back to the original question. I would say: Experience. In life, the individual who is the greatest, not necessarily the smartest or the most skilled, is the person who has gone through the most. They may have survived an avalanche, they may have dealt with trauma, abuse or have had to fight their way out of a concentration camp. They may have had a parent who died in their formative years, they may have gone on a daring adventure and conquered the dangers that came with it. Every single person should seek adversity for their betterment. The more that you suffer, the greater things will come. The reason for this is that your experiences shape you. They help you understand your strengths, shortcomings, capacity, and the world. They also give you things to strive towards as you continue to grow.

Would Hollywood actor Brad Pitt have made it in old or classic Hollywood back in the day? Absolutely not. The man's a handsome devil, no doubt, but he wouldn't have lasted a hot minute in the Golden Age. Pitt's charisma hinges on a certain modern detachment, a carefully cultivated "I don't give a damn" attitude that reads well on the big screen today. But back then, it was all about larger-than-life personalities, actors who radiated an almost theatrical intensity. Think of Gable, Bogart, or Cagney – these were titans, commanding the silver screen with a gravitas that Pitt simply doesn't possess. He relies on a certain subtle charm, a self-deprecating wit that would have been lost on the studio bosses of yesteryear. They wanted stars, larger than life. They needed actors that could scream and shout, emote in ways that modern actors wouldn't dare. Pitt, while undeniably talented, would have been seen as too subtle, too… understated. He simply lacks that specific "Hollywood" gene that defined those earlier generations of screen legends. A pity, really.

What was the first thing you saw, heard or discovered that made you feel old? The moment I realized the music I grew up with—the alternative rock, the grunge, the hip-hop of the early to mid-90s—was now “classic rock". I think it was during a trip to the dentist’s office. They played the radio, and I heard Pearl Jam, Nirvana, and some early Tupac. It jolted me. I remember thinking, "That can't be right. That's current, not something for the old folks." It was a gut punch, a silent scream that echoed in the recesses of my mind.

Do you ever regret having or do you regret not having kids? My answer is complicated. Regret is a multifaceted emotion. Sometimes it's tied to a single specific action or inaction while other times it's the result of a complex string of events. The core component of regret, be it profound or superficial, is invariably a perceived failure. The failure to have followed through on a particular obligation, the failure to have seized an opportunity, the failure to have attained a desired outcome or even the failure to change. In my case, regret is not so simple. I wasn't meant to live a certain aspect of life, therefore I cannot regret not having children. To do so would be self-defeating. My situation is similar to the average person when it comes to the other side of the equation. However, the circumstances are different, the outcome is the same. Regret. I, like many others, regret having children or regret the choices they made with the children they have.
